confirmed.title: spectralExcessPeak's default threshold + unweighted residual search reports a form population in 100% of featureless red-noise fields
confirmed.description: Two compounding problems. (a) The residual search at :352-356 takes the max of `ys[i] - (intercept + slope*xs[i])` over all bins with no weighting by bin population. `count[r]` is 8 modes at k=1 but 380 at k=60, so the chi-square scatter of a bin's log10 mean is 0.153 at k=1 versus 0.022 at k=60 — the max residual is systematically drawn to the lowest wavenumbers, i.e. back toward the window size, which is exactly the failure mode this function was written to replace. (b) Because OLS residuals sum to zero, `max(residual)` is always >= 0, so `excessRatio = 10^best.residual` is always >= 1 and the shipped default `minExcessRatio = 1.05` is far below the noise floor. The test suite only pins the negative case with an explicitly overridden `minExcessRatio: 3` (tests/instrument-descriptors.test.js:238); the live caller fieldSampler.js:173 uses the 1.05 default. The concept is sound — with a genuine band-limited population the metric is excellent (10/10 seeds returned 71.4 km against a 70.7 km truth) — it is the threshold and the unweighted argmax that fail.
confirmed.failureScenario: Using the exact live probe geometry (128x128 over a 2000 km patch, spectral slope -3.9 which is the slope measured on the live lab field) over 40 reseeds of PURE scale-free noise containing no band-limited population at all: `detected` came back true 40/40 (excessRatio 1.58 to 3.95, mean 2.28), and `formWavelength` had mean 707 km, sd 299 km, CV 42%, range 125-1000 km, with 25/40 peaks landing at k<=3 (>=667 km on a 2000 km window). So `describeSample` sets `d.formDetected = true` and emits a `formWavelength` on every probe of ordinary terrain, and `screenWavelengthProxy` (world-engine-lab.html) multiplies that noise-driven number by the disc scale and reports it as an on-screen form size.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Weight the residual search by bin population (search `residual * sqrt(count[r])`, or equivalently require the residual to clear ~2 * 0.434/sqrt(count[r]) in log10), return `count` per bin from radialPSD so the caller can compute it, and raise the default minExcessRatio to a value calibrated against the measured null (the 40-seed null run above suggests >= 3, matching what the test already had to pass in by hand).
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Could not refute; reproduced independently three ways.

(b) THRESHOLD IS BELOW THE NULL FLOOR — proven analytically and empirically. leastSquaresSlope (descriptors.js:368-376) is OLS and the intercept at descriptors.js:351 is the OLS intercept (meanY - slope*meanX), so residuals sum to zero (measured 6.71e-14). Therefore max(residual) >= 0 and excessRatio = 10^best.residual >= 1 unconditionally. Over 200 pure-power-law realisations at the exact live geometry (128x128 / 2000 km, PSD slope -3.9), the null excessRatio ranged 1.29-5.21, median 2.10 — the shipped minExcessRatio = 1.05 (descriptors.js:340) sits below the null MINIMUM, giving detected=true 200/200. False-positive rate by threshold: 1.05 -> 100%, 2 -> 60%, 3 -> 13%, 4 -> 3%, 6 -> 0%.

SMOKING GUN: the repo's own fixture at tests/instrument-descriptors.test.js:194-241, named "declines to report a form size for pure scale-free noise", returns detected=true / excessRatio 1.69 / wavelength 128 km when invoked the way the live caller invokes it. The test passes ONLY because line 238 overrides { minExcessRatio: 3 }. fieldSampler.js:173 calls spectralExcessPeak(h, grid) with no options, so no test covers the shipped default.

(a) UNWEIGHTED ARGMAX IS PULLED TO THE WINDOW SCALE — confirmed. Over 200 null realisations the peak landed at k<=3 (>=667 km on a 2000 km window) 74% of the time vs ~5% expected if uniform over the 64 bins. Dividing each residual by that bin's expected log-scatter (0.434/sqrt(count[r])) drops it to 12%, isolating the missing population weighting as the cause. This reproduces the window-size artefact descriptors.js:324-329 says the function exists to eliminate.

LIVE CORROBORATION: docs/WORKSTREAMS/nonvisual-analysis-channel-2026-07-24/evidence/AC-SAMPLE-live.md reports R=0.5 and R=1 as excessRatio 1.94/2.39 with form size 1000 km (k=2, half the window) — dead centre of the measured null. The doc's prose calls those "the metric declining, correctly" while the shipped detected flag returns true for both. Code contradicts its own evidence doc.

REFUTATIONS ATTEMPTED, ALL FAILED: (1) "documented choice" — descriptors.js:336-338 asserts "1.0 = no excess at all, i.e. no detectable feature population", which is mathematically unreachable given zero-sum OLS residuals, so the header's premise is itself wrong rather than a deliberate design note; (2) "caller must check excessRatio" — the function ships its own verdict and fieldSampler.js:176 re-exports it as d.formDetected; (3) "downstream gates it" — world-engine-lab.html:6796 checks formWavelength != null, NOT formDetected, so screenWavelengthProxy multiplies the noise-driven number by sVisNow unconditionally (NaN != null is also true, so the NaN path leaks too); (4) "laws.js catches it" — laws.js never consumes formWavelength, it audits pure functions only. Only partial mitigation found: sweep.js planSweep/cvIsMeaningful (lines 100-114, 168-170) would expose the 41-62% CV, so a multi-seed SWEEP conclusion is not silently false — that bounds blast radius but does not touch the single-probe false positive or screenWavelengthProxy.

My first synthesis used fixed-amplitude modes, which UNDERSTATES real periodogram scatter; adding true Rayleigh amplitude scatter widened the null (max 3.43 -> 5.21), so live terrain is worse than the conservative measurement, not better.

SEVERITY: high stands. Read-only instrument, no render impact, and raw excessRatio is still exposed — but the headline "how big are the forms" answer is a false positive on 100% of ordinary-terrain probes, it recreates the precise artefact the function replaced, its own null test gives false assurance by overriding the default, and its own live evidence table already contains two misclassified rows.

FIX (two separable changes): weight the residual search by sqrt(count[r]) as a per-bin z-score instead of a raw argmax, and raise the default to >= 4 or derive it from the measured null rather than pinning a constant. Fixing only the threshold leaves the low-k pull on genuine detections.

confirmed.title: shiftSignificance coerces a NaN standard error to zero, so single-sample ensembles report significant movement
confirmed.description: `const combined = Math.sqrt((a.sem || 0) ** 2 + (b.sem || 0) ** 2)`. NaN is falsy in JavaScript, so `NaN || 0` evaluates to 0. `meanSEM` deliberately returns `sem: NaN` for n < 2 (:35) precisely to say 'this ensemble has no measurable uncertainty' — and this line silently converts that statement into 'this ensemble has ZERO uncertainty'. That inverts the meaning of the one guard the module has, in the file whose entire stated purpose is to stop two random draws being called a signal.
confirmed.failureScenario: shiftSignificance([10.0], [10.0000001]) returns { moved: true, sigma: Infinity } — a 1e-8 float wobble between two single samples reported as an infinitely significant regression. The mixed case is worse because it looks plausible: shiftSignificance([10, 10.1, 9.9, 10.05], [10.2]) returns { moved: true, sigma: 4.39 }. If the second ensemble had the same population spread as the first, the honest combined SEM is 0.095 and sigma is 1.97 — below the z=2 bar, i.e. NOT moved. The coercion flips the verdict.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Treat a non-finite SEM as undecidable rather than as zero: if either ensemble has n < 2, return { moved: false, sigma: NaN, reason: 'ensemble of size 1 carries no uncertainty — at least 2 seeds per side are required' }. Only take the zero-combined-SEM branch when both ensembles have n >= 2 and both genuinely measured sd = 0.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:

Ran the exact claimed inputs against the real module:
- shiftSignificance([10.0],[10.0000001]) -> {moved:true, sigma:Infinity, delta:1e-7}
- shiftSignificance([10,10.1,9.9,10.05],[10.2]) -> {moved:true, sigma:4.3915, fractionalDelta:0.0187, current:{n:1, sem:NaN}}
Both match the claim.

Refutation attempts all fail:
(1) Not out-of-contract: sweep.js:39 explicitly accepts M=1 seeds ("need at least 1 seed"), so single-sample ensembles are a sanctioned input to the instrument.
(2) Not a documented deliberate choice: nothing in the header (stats.js:1-21) or the shiftSignificance docstring (:171-175) mentions single samples. The only stated intent is the opposite — tests/instrument-descriptors.test.js:384 pins meanSEM([42]).sem as NaN under the title "reports no uncertainty for a single sample rather than inventing one". Line 178 inverts exactly that guard.
(3) The !(combined > 0) branch (:181-183) does not cover it honestly: meanSEM([10,10]) legitimately returns sem:0 with n:2 (a real zero-spread measurement), so the coercion collapses "unknown uncertainty" into the same branch as "measured zero uncertainty".
(4) The Infinity tell only exists in the pure 1-vs-1 case. The mixed case returns sigma 4.39 with no marker at all — indistinguishable in shape from the honest 4-vs-4 result (which I measured at sigma 3.31), so a 1-seed follow-up outranks a properly sampled one in the module's own "rank what moved most" ordering.
(5) A caller could inspect the returned baseline/current n and sem, but `moved` is the module's declared decision output and the file's whole thesis (:8-18) is that the decision layer must be able to report UNRESOLVABLE rather than fake a call; delegating resolvability to the caller is the very failure mode documented there.

Nuance against the reviewer: their "honest sigma 1.97" assumes the single-sample ensemble shares the baseline's population spread — an extra assumption. The defensible output is a third state / moved:false-with-reason, not necessarily 1.97. The verdict flip stands regardless.

Severity lowered high -> medium: grep across the repo finds shiftSignificance referenced only at stats.js:176 and in tests/instrument-descriptors.test.js — no production caller, not wired into world-engine-lab.html or laws.js. So nothing currently shipped emits a wrong number; this is a latent correctness defect in an exported public API. Fix is a one-liner: treat non-finite sem as unresolvable (e.g. return {moved:false, sigma:NaN, reason:'ensemble has no uncertainty estimate (n<2)'}) instead of coercing to 0.

confirmed.title: fitPowerLaw returns exponentSE = 0 for a 2-point fit, defeating the entire three-valued verdict system
confirmed.description: `const dof = Math.max(n - 2, 1); const seB = Math.sqrt((sw / denom) * (chi2 / dof));`. With n = 2 and 2 free parameters the residuals are identically zero, so chi2 = 0 and seB collapses to ~1e-15 regardless of how noisy the two input points actually were. The `Math.max(n - 2, 1)` guard prevents a division by zero but does so by asserting one degree of freedom that does not exist. lawVerdict then falls through to its 1e-9 float-noise floor (:148) — a floor written for the genuinely deterministic case — and renders a hard PASS/FAIL. The instrument cannot distinguish 'this law is exact' from 'I had no degrees of freedom', which is the precise class of error the UNRESOLVABLE verdict exists to catch. Reachable without a 2-value sweep: responseCurve filters each descriptor's points to finite y at sweep.js:73, so any descriptor that only resolves at 2 of N driver values gets a zero-SE fit.
confirmed.failureScenario: fitPowerLaw([{x:1, y:1.0, sem:0.3}, {x:2, y:2.05, sem:0.3}]) returns exponent 1.0356, exponentSE 1.43e-15, r2 = 1 — despite input SEMs of 30% that make the exponent uncertain by roughly +/-0.6. lawVerdict against a claimed exponent of 1 returns FAIL; against a claimed 2 it also returns FAIL. The correct answer in both cases is UNRESOLVABLE.
confirmed.suggestedFix: When n <= 2, or whenever chi2/dof underflows, fall back to the input-error-propagated variance sw/denom without the reduced-chi-square rescaling (the input SEMs are already available and are the real uncertainty), and return exponentSE = NaN when n < 3 and no input SEMs were supplied so lawVerdict correctly reports UNRESOLVABLE.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
CONFIRMED — I could not refute it; I reproduced it end-to-end.

MECHANISM (stats.js:97-100). With n=2 and 2 free parameters the log-log fit passes exactly through both points, so chi2 is identically 0 and `seB = Math.sqrt((sw / denom) * (chi2 / dof))` collapses to float residue. Running the reviewer's literal input `fitPowerLaw([{x:1,y:1.0,sem:0.3},{x:2,y:2.05,sem:0.3}])` returns `{exponent: 1.0356239097307198, exponentSE: 1.4286653110964323e-15, r2: 1, n: 2}` — the claimed numbers verbatim.

THE GUARD IS CAUSALLY LOAD-BEARING. `const dof = Math.max(n - 2, 1)` (stats.js:99) is not incidental. With a true dof of 0, `chi2/dof` would be 0/0 = NaN, `exponentSE` would be NaN, and `lawVerdict` would correctly return UNRESOLVABLE via its own non-finite guard at stats.js:137-139. The guard is precisely what converts a would-be-UNRESOLVABLE into a hard PASS/FAIL through the 1e-9 float-noise floor at stats.js:148.

THE CODE CONTRADICTS ITS OWN STATED INTENT. stats.js:95-96 says the chi-square scaling exists "so that under-estimated input errors inflate the reported uncertainty rather than hiding in it." At n=2 the input errors are entirely hidden. The correct propagated slope SE is already computed on that same line — `sqrt(sw / denom)` evaluates to 0.4816 for the reviewer's input (I computed it). The code multiplies that real, correct number by zero and discards it.

REACHABLE VIA THE REAL PATH, NOT ONLY A HAND-MADE CALL. I drove it through `responseCurve` with a descriptor that resolves at only 2 of 3 driver values (the per-descriptor finite filter at sweep.js:73) over 5 seeds with genuine spread: result `{exponent: 1, exponentSE: 0, r2: 1, n: 2}` with real per-point SEMs of 0.1437 and 0.2874, producing `resolvingPower: 0` and a hard FAIL. Partial data is an anticipated, designed-for condition (sweep.js:55-59, "a single failed reading must not kill a long sweep"), and sweep.js:39 explicitly accepts 2 driver values as a valid sweep.

A VERDICT ACTUALLY INVERTS. Against a claimed exponent of 1, the code returns FAIL. With the propagated SE of 0.4816, |1.0356 - 1| = 0.0356 against a 2-sigma tolerance of 0.963 — comfortably consistent with the claim. (The reviewer's stated "correct answer = UNRESOLVABLE" is slightly off: dNull = 1.0356 vs tol = 0.963 makes it marginally PASS. The inversion is real; only their label for the honest verdict is imprecise.)

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED. No header comment or contract restricts fits to n>=3 — I read all of stats.js, sweep.js and laws.js. laws.js:159-163 hands `fit.exponentSE` straight into `lawVerdict` with no `n` check, discarding `fit.n` into a display-only `points` field. The instrument's own tests teach the vulnerable pattern (tests/instrument-sweep.test.js:73, 183, 194 all call `lawVerdict({measuredSE: fit.exponentSE})` on a `responseCurve` fit).

SEVERITY DOWNGRADE high -> medium. I ran `auditLaws()`: all six registered laws evaluate 7 points (laws.js:69-127), so the only in-repo consumer of `lawVerdict` is unaffected today, and no shipped path auto-renders a verdict from a 2-point field sweep. `_lab.responseCurve` returns fits to the console and the result object does expose `n: 2` to an attentive reader. "Defeating the entire three-valued verdict system" overstates present impact. It remains a genuine defect because this is a measurement instrument whose stated raison d'etre (stats.js:8-21) is refusing to overstate confidence, and it silently reports SE ~ 1e-15 with r2 = 1 for a fit that has zero degrees of freedom — with the correct propagated SE already sitting in the same expression. Note n=3 degrades gracefully (dof=1, chi2 > 0); n=2 is the singular case, accompanied by an always-`r2: 1` that is a second overconfidence signal.

Fix shape (not requested, one line): report `sqrt(sw/denom) * sqrt(max(chi2/dof, 1))` when points carry real SEMs, or return `exponentSE: NaN` when `n < 3` so the existing non-finite guard routes it to UNRESOLVABLE.

confirmed.title: shiftSignificance treats an unknown SEM as zero uncertainty, so single-reading ensembles get infinite significance
confirmed.description: `const combined = Math.sqrt((a.sem || 0) ** 2 + (b.sem || 0) ** 2)` — meanSEM returns `sem: NaN` for n<2 (stats.js:35), and **NaN is falsy**, so `NaN || 0` collapses an unknown uncertainty to zero rather than to "unmeasured". Both-sides-n=1 then takes the zero-SEM branch (stats.js:181-183) and returns `{moved: true, sigma: Infinity}`. One-sided n=1 is just as bad and quieter: the unknown side contributes 0 and sigma is computed from the other ensemble's SEM alone. This is the decision rule of the regression channel, in a module whose own thesis (sweep.js:13-16) is that a single reading measures the seed as much as the driver.
confirmed.failureScenario: Verified by execution: `shiftSignificance([50.0], [50.7])` returns `{ moved: true, delta: 0.7, sigma: Infinity, baseline:{n:1,sem:NaN}, current:{n:1,sem:NaN} }` — two single procedural readings that differ only by seed noise are reported as a regression at infinite confidence. And `shiftSignificance([50], [48,52,53,51,49])` returns sigma = 0.647, computed as delta / current.sem (0.6 / 0.9274) with the baseline's uncertainty silently dropped.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Guard on `Number.isFinite`, not truthiness, and refuse rather than assume: if either ensemble has n<2, return `{ moved: null, sigma: NaN, reason: 'ensemble of size 1 carries no uncertainty — cannot test a shift' }`. Reserve the zero-SEM branch for genuinely zero *measured* spread (n>=2, sd===0), and even there prefer `moved: null` over `sigma: Infinity`. Also add `fractionalDelta` to that branch's return so the result shape is stable (stats.js:182 omits it).
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Could not refute; reproduced by execution. stats.js:178 `Math.sqrt((a.sem || 0) ** 2 + (b.sem || 0) ** 2)` coerces an unmeasured SEM to zero, because meanSEM returns `sem: NaN` for n<2 (stats.js:33,35) and NaN is falsy. Executed against the real module: `shiftSignificance([50.0],[50.7])` returns sigma === Infinity, moved: true, baseline.sem NaN, n 1 (the `!(combined > 0)` branch at stats.js:181-183). Decisively, the sibling function in the SAME file handles the identical input class the opposite way — lawVerdict:137 routes a non-finite measuredSE to UNRESOLVABLE rather than treating it as zero. (3) Not unreachable: no docstring or guard requires n>=2 (docstring stats.js:171-175 says only "two ensembles"), and sweep.js:40 explicitly permits M=1 sweeps, which produce exactly these sem:NaN ensembles. Severity lowered high -> medium: repo-wide grep (js/html/md/mjs, excluding node_modules) finds shiftSignificance only at stats.js:176 and tests/instrument-descriptors.test.js — no lab wiring, no production caller, so no report today is wrong. confirmed.title: z=2 is documented as ~95% but exponentSE is a small-dof external error estimate — a law that is exactly true FAILs 22% of the time at the lab's defaults
confirmed.description: `seB = sqrt((sw/denom) * (chi2/dof))` with `dof = n-2` makes the reported SE an *external* (residual-based) estimate. An interval built as measured ± z*SE from such an estimate follows Student's t with n-2 dof, not the normal, yet DEFAULT_Z is fixed at 2 and stats.js:23 states '2 sigma ~ 95%'. At the lab's default sweep (world-engine-lab.html:6820-6821 → N=6 values, M=3 seeds) the true two-sided coverage of ±2*SE is ~88%, and at N=3 values (dof=1) it is ~70%. Because lawVerdict FAILs whenever |measured - claimed| > z*SE (stats.js:149), the miscalibration converts directly into false FAILs. Two compounding causes: (a) no t-correction; (b) at M=3 the 1/sem^2 weights are themselves built from a 2-dof variance estimate, which is heavy-tailed, so the reported SE is biased low.
confirmed.failureScenario: Monte Carlo over the module's own code (4000 trials each, y = 10*x^0.5 with independent lognormal-ish seed noise cv=0.25, VALUES=[0.5,1,2,4,8,16], claimed=0.5 i.e. the law is EXACTLY true): M=3 -> FAIL 22.3%; M=5 -> 18.1%; M=10 -> 13.6%; M=30 -> 11.2%. It does not converge to 5% with more seeds because the deficit is in the fit's dof (N-2=4, t-coverage 88.4%), not in M. With N=3 driver values: FAIL 34.4% at M=3 and 29.9% at M=10. Separately, the mean reported exponentSE at M=3 is 0.0448 against a true across-reseed SD of the exponent of 0.0666 — the instrument understates its own uncertainty by 33%. Net effect: an operator running the default `_lab.responseCurve()` against a correct law sees a red FAIL roughly one run in five, which is precisely the 'the failure was a property of the ruler' incident this file was written to prevent (stats.js:8-11).
confirmed.suggestedFix: Replace the fixed z with a coverage-driven multiplier: return `dof` from fitPowerLaw and have lawVerdict use t_{1-alpha/2, dof} (2.78 at n=6, 12.71 at n=3) instead of 2, or at minimum return `dof` and `coverage` in the verdict so 'PASS/FAIL at 95%' is not asserted when it is 88% or 70%. Widening N (more driver values) buys more than widening M for the exponent test, and the verdict text should say so.

confirmed.title: fitPowerLaw silently gives points with no usable SEM a weight of 1, which is not on the 1/sigma^2 scale — the point is effectively dropped while n/dropped report it as included
confirmed.description: `const s = ... p.sem > 0 ? p.sem / p.y : 0; return s > 0 ? 1/(s*s) : 1;` mixes two incommensurable scales. A point with a real SEM gets weight (y/sem)^2 — for the lab's default M=3 at cv=0.25 that is ~48, and for a tight ensemble it can be 10^4 — while a point whose SEM is NaN or 0 gets weight 1, i.e. an implicit assumption of 100% relative error. In responseCurve a point reaches n=1 (sem NaN) whenever the tolerated-failure path fires for all but one seed (sweep.js:55-59), and sem is exactly 0 whenever an integer-valued descriptor like bandCount (fieldSampler.js:180) returns the same value for every seed. The result is a point that is arithmetically excluded from the fit but reported inside `n` with `dropped: 0`.
confirmed.failureScenario: Verified by execution. Points [{x:1,y:10,sem:0.05},{x:2,y:20,sem:0.1},{x:4,y:40,sem:0.2},{x:8,y:60,sem:NaN}] — the last point is off the y=10x line, and it is the long lever arm at the end of the x-range. Correctly weighted (giving the last point the same 0.5% relative error as the others) the fit is exponent 0.875 +/- 0.0719, r2 0.987. As written it returns exponent 0.99999 +/- 0.00104, r2 0.99999, `n: 4, dropped: 0` — a 14% shift in the exponent and a 69x shrink of the error bar, presented as a tighter, better fit over all four points. Fed to lawVerdict against a claimed exponent of 1, that is a hard PASS on a curve that is actually 0.875.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Do not mix scales. Either (a) require all-or-nothing: if any usable point lacks a finite positive SEM, fall back to uniform weights for every point and say so in the return; or (b) impute the missing sigma from the pooled relative scatter of the points that do have one, never the literal 1. Either way, return `weightsUniform: true/false` and count SEM-less points in a new `unweighted` field so a reader can see that a point contributed nothing.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
CONFIRMED by execution against the real modules; I could not refute it on any of five angles.

THE CODE (stats.js:82-85): `const s = Number.isFinite(p.sem) && p.sem > 0 ? p.sem / p.y : 0; return s > 0 ? 1/(s*s) : 1;` — points with a usable SEM get weight (y/sem)^2; points without get literal 1. Two incommensurable scales in one weight vector.

REACHABILITY (refutation attempt 2 failed). sweep.js:74 passes sems from meanSEM straight into fitPowerLaw; the only filter (sweep.js:73) tests `y`, never `sem`. world-engine-lab.html:6818-6836 invokes this with default `seeds:[1,2,3]` and no guard. Two live sources of unusable sem:
  - sem === 0 exactly: descriptors that agree across all M seeds. `formDetected` (fieldSampler.js:176) is a boolean flattened to 1/0 at sweep.js:150 and is present in the DEFAULT patch probe; `bandCount` (fieldSampler.js:180) is an integer. Both give sd=0 -> sem=0 at some driver values and sem>0 at others.
  - sem === NaN: meanSEM line 35 returns NaN for n<2, reached whenever the tolerated-failure path (sweep.js:55-59) drops all but one seed at a value.

DOCUMENTED-CHOICE DEFENSE FAILS (attempt 1). The docstring at stats.js:63-69 affirmatively promises 1/sigma^2 weighting "so a noisy radius point cannot drag the exponent as hard as a clean one," and says nothing about a fallback. The sem===0 branch INVERTS that stated invariant: the perfectly determined point receives weight 1, the lowest in the set, while a noisy neighbour receives 676 or 1369.

CHI2 INFLATION DOES NOT COVER IT (attempt 3). stats.js:95-100 comments that under-estimated input errors inflate the SE. Measured: the SE shrinks 5x to 69x, it does not inflate.

BLAST RADIUS NARROWED BUT NOT REFUTED (attempt 4). laws.js:157 pushes {x, y} with no sem at all, so the law-registry path gets uniform weight 1 = plain OLS, which is correct. The defect is confined to the field/responseCurve channel.

MEASURED CONSEQUENCES (all executed):
  - Reviewer's example reproduces exactly: as-written 0.9999896 +/- 0.001038, r2 0.99998, n:4, dropped:0; proportional-sem 0.8754888 +/- 0.071887, r2 0.98670.
  - CORRECTION TO THE REVIEWER: their own example does NOT flip the verdict. lawVerdict against claimed 1 returns PASS for both (tol = 2*0.0719 = 0.1438 > |0.8755-1| = 0.1245). The stated "hard PASS on a curve that is actually 0.875" consequence is overstated for that input.
  - But realistic inputs DO flip it. Integer bandCount ensembles [3,3,3],[4,4,4],[6,6,6],[8,9,9],[12,12,13] (truth exponent 0.5) produce weights [1,1,1,676,1369]: as-written 0.5097 +/- 0.00262 -> FAIL against claimed 0.5; uniform weights 0.5195 +/- 0.01400 -> PASS. A FALSE FAIL driven by an over-tight error bar is precisely the read-gate failure class stats.js:8-21 says this module exists to eliminate.
  - Second realistic case, where the seed-starved point is where a clamp binds (the exact worry stated at laws.js:125-127): as-written 0.5895 +/- 0.03945, r2 0.9911; uniform 0.4296 +/- 0.09888, r2 0.9042. A 37% exponent shift with a 2.5x tighter bar and a HIGHER r2 — the fit looks cleaner precisely because it discarded the point carrying the physics.
  - Influence check: at the lab's M=3 with cv~0.25 the finite-sem weights are ~48-64 while the unusable-sem point sits at 1 (~1.5% influence, reported as n:4, dropped:0). With tighter ensembles the ratio reaches 1:40000 (0.0008% influence).

SEVERITY high stands. This sits on the live field-measurement path that feeds lawVerdict, silently changes fitted exponents and shrinks reported uncertainty by 5-69x, and can flip a verdict to a false FAIL — the over-confident-verdict failure mode this file was written to prevent. `n`/`dropped` reporting is arguably accurate to its own narrow documented meaning (dropped = non-positive x or y), but the numeric result is not.

confirmed.title: fitPowerLaw fabricates a degree of freedom at n=2, returning SE ~ 1e-16 and an absolutely confident verdict on a zero-dof fit
confirmed.description: `const dof = Math.max(n - 2, 1)` turns the zero degrees of freedom of a two-point straight-line fit into one. A line through two points is exact, so chi2 = 0, so seB = 0 (up to float residue), so lawVerdict's tolerance collapses to the 1e-9 floor (stats.js:148) and every verdict becomes maximally confident. responseCurve explicitly permits exactly two driver values (sweep.js:39 rejects only <2), and n also falls to 2 in the field layer without any unusual input: sweep.js:73 filters out points whose mean is non-finite, and formWavelength is NaN whenever spectralExcessPeak cannot build a spectrum (descriptors.js:343-345), so a 6-value sweep with 4 undetected peaks fits 2 points.
confirmed.failureScenario: Verified by execution: `fitPowerLaw([{x:1,y:10},{x:2,y:14}])` returns `{exponent: 0.4854, exponentSE: 9.06e-16, r2: 1, n: 2}`, and `lawVerdict({measured: 0.4854, measuredSE: 9.06e-16, claimed: 2})` returns `verdict: 'FAIL', reason: 'measured 0.485 differs from claimed 2 by 1.515, beyond 2x its standard error (0.000)'`. The correct answer for a two-point fit is UNRESOLVABLE — the data cannot constrain a slope and its uncertainty simultaneously. The same mechanism grants a hard PASS with r2 = 1 when the two points happen to lie on the claimed law.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Return `exponentSE: NaN` (and a `dof: 0` field) when n < 3, so lawVerdict's existing non-finite branch (stats.js:137-139) reports UNRESOLVABLE with 'two points cannot constrain a slope and its uncertainty'. Keep `exponent` — the slope is still the best estimate — but never pair it with a fabricated error bar. Consider also raising responseCurve's minimum to 3 driver values, since 2 can never produce a resolvable exponent.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
I tried to refute this on four fronts (unreachable input, documented-deliberate-choice, no live verdict path, wrong mechanism). Three of the four partly landed, but the core defect survives and I reproduced it end-to-end through the real `responseCurve` pipeline with realistic field data, not just the isolated function.

WHAT SURVIVES REFUTATION

`seB = Math.sqrt((sw / denom) * (chi2 / dof))` (stats.js:100) multiplies the propagated variance `sw/denom` by the reduced chi-square. When residuals vanish, the per-point SEMs are annihilated regardless of how large they are. `fitPowerLaw([{x:1,y:10,sem:5},{x:2,y:14,sem:7}])` returns the identical `exponentSE: 9.06e-16` as the no-sem call — the supplied uncertainties have zero effect on the reported uncertainty.

Reachability in the field layer, verified by execution through the real pipeline. `responseCurve` supplies genuine per-point SEMs (sweep.js:72) and drops points whose mean is non-finite (sweep.js:73); `fitPowerLaw` further drops points with y <= 0 (stats.js:74). A descriptor this codebase itself documents as sign-straddling — sweep.js:164-166 says "An elevation field centred near zero has a mean of ~0.006 against a spread of ~0.03" — is emitted as `elevation.mean` at fieldSampler.js:199 and flattened to `elevation.mean` by sweep.js:151. A 6-value / 5-seed sweep at the lab's own default `values` (world-engine-lab.html:6820, `[0.5,1,2,4,8,16]`) where that mean is positive at two radii and negative at four produced:

  fit: {"exponent":0.270,"exponentSE":0,"r2":1,"n":2,"dropped":4}
  per-point sem at the surviving points: 8.58e-5  (real, finite, discarded)
  lawVerdict(...claimed:2) -> verdict "FAIL", "beyond 2x its standard error (0.000)"

That is a maximally confident FAIL on two points, with each point's real uncertainty thrown away. `elevation.skew` (fieldSampler.js:199) straddles zero the same way. This route is more reachable than the NaN-formWavelength route the claim cites, which needs `spec.length < 4` (descriptors.js:343) and cannot happen on the default 128x128 patch.

The "deliberate documented choice" defense does not cover this case. stats.js:142-148 justifies the 1e-9 tolerance floor for "auditing a deterministic pure function, where every point lies exactly on the law" — where zero uncertainty is TRUE. The field layer is explicitly not that (sweep.js:12-18 on why M seeds is non-negotiable), and reporting SE=0 there contradicts the file's own opening contract at stats.js:5, "Every number this module returns carries its own uncertainty," and the whole UNRESOLVABLE rationale at stats.js:8-21.

WHERE THE CLAIM IS WRONG — corrections that should ride with the finding

1. `Math.max(n - 2, 1)` (stats.js:99) is NOT the root cause. Verified: `fitPowerLaw([{x:1,y:1,sem:0.5},{x:2,y:4,sem:2},{x:4,y:16,sem:8}])` returns `exponentSE: 0` at n=3, where dof=1 and the clamp is inert. Removing the clamp would turn n=2 into NaN/Infinity -> UNRESOLVABLE via stats.js:137, but would leave the n>=3 collinear case exactly as over-confident. The fix belongs at the seB formula (floor the SE at the propagated `sqrt(sw/denom)`, or require n>2 for chi-square scaling), not at the dof clamp.

2. Not reachable in the law-registry layer. Every entry in LAW_REGISTRY declares 7 driver values (laws.js:69,79,94,105,115,127) over deterministic, always-finite pure functions, and laws.js:157 drops only non-finite y. The sole production `lawVerdict` call site (laws.js:160) therefore never sees n=2.

3. No production code auto-composes a verdict on a sweep fit. `lawVerdict` appears only at laws.js:160 and in tests; the sweep path returns `fits` as data. The confident-verdict step is operator-driven at the console — though that composition is exactly what the suite demonstrates as the intended usage (tests/instrument-sweep.test.js:73,183,194), so it is a real workflow, not a contrived one.

4. Partial self-disclosure the claim omits: the returned object carries `n: 2` and `dropped: 4` alongside the fabricated SE, so a reader who checks n is not deceived.

SEVERITY. "high" overstates it. The instrument is read-only — no rendered frame, no golden, no shipped gate consumes this. The degeneracy is disclosed via n/dropped in the same object, and the law-audit layer is immune. But it does produce a confidently wrong number in the one module whose stated purpose is to never overstate confidence, on an input the lab's own default sweep can hit. Medium.
